traveler: Abu Yazid Tayfur ibn Isa al-Bistami (Bayazid Bastami)
title: The Man Who Did Not Travel: Bestam, the Sealed Room, and the Four Words Persian Could Not Put Down
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bestam, the grandfather leaves the fire
stops.date_confidence: undated. Sahlaji gives the conversion only as family background and fixes no year; the date here is an ordering device, not a datum
stops.campa: In the province of Qumes, under the northern wall of the Alborz, a Zoroastrian named Surushan gives up the fire and takes the shahada. His three sons, Adam, Ali, and Isa, grow up in the new religion and carry it further than their father can have meant: all three live as ascetics in Bestam, in the quarter where the fire-priests still keep their houses. Isa's son will be born into that quarter, a Muslim among the mobedan, one generation removed from the altar. Sahlaji records the conversion in a line and gives it no date. Nobody writes down the year the fire went out.
suggested_refs: The Mo'bedan quarter of Bestam, named for the Zoroastrian priesthood the family came out of
sources: Gerhard Bowering, 'Bestami, Bayazid,' Encyclopaedia Iranica (1989), citing Sahlaji

stops.name: Bestam, birth in the quarter of the fire-priests
stops.date_confidence: no birth year survives. The printed c. 804 is a modern back-calculation from the 261/875 death date; Sahlaji implies 161/777 and Abd al-Rafi 131/748, and the three are mutually exclusive
stops.campa: Abu Yazid Tayfur ibn Isa ibn Surushan is born in the Mo'bedan quarter of Bestam. The name the world will use is Bayazid, and the town's name will follow him as al-Bistami through every language Sufism is afterward written in. Of the birth itself nothing is recorded, not the year and not the season. Bowering opens the standard account by saying that historical evidence for his life is sparse, and the sparseness begins at the first fact. The house is known and the quarter is known. The date is somebody's later arithmetic.
suggested_refs: Sahlaji, Ketab al-nur men kalemat Abi Tayfur, p. 47, the earliest surviving account of the household
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid,' citing Sahlaji p. 47
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bayezid-i Bistami'

stops.name: Balkh, the ascetic of tawakkul takes the eastern road
stops.date_confidence: Shaqiq dies in 194/810. A Bayazid born c. 804 could not have received him, which is exactly why Iranica reads this meeting as circumstantial evidence for the earlier death date of 848
stops.campa: Shaqiq of Balkh, who teaches that a man should hold nothing back for tomorrow because God is the only provision worth carrying, comes west out of the Oxus country and is received at Bestam by the young Bayazid, in the company of Abu Torab of Nakhshab. Afterward the two keep up a correspondence by messenger along the Khorasan road. Shaqiq dies the following year on the frontier. Three centuries and more later Baha ud-Din Walad will be born in this same Balkh and carry its learning west to Anatolia; the road between the two towns is already old when Bayazid is a boy.
suggested_refs: Shaqiq al-Balkhi's doctrine of tawakkul, reliance, the seed of the Khorasani ascetic school
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji pp. 91, 95; Sebt b. al-Jawzi, Mer'at al-zaman p. 163; Attar, Tadhkerat al-awliya I p. 147
baha_ud_din_walad.journey.json, stop 'Balkh, the birth of Baha ud-Din Walad'

stops.name: Bestam, the Hanafite books
stops.date_confidence: undated. Iranica records the legal training without a year or a teacher's name
stops.campa: Before the ecstasies there is jurisprudence. The boy studies Hanafite law, the school of the Persian east, and learns the exact measure of ablution, the hours of prayer, the divisions of an inheritance. It marks him for life. He will rinse his mouth and wash his tongue before he lets the name of God across it, and he will drive a man out of the mosque of Bestam for standing to pray without a proper washing. The one who will answer the call to prayer by saying that he is greater begins as a jurist counting the bows.
suggested_refs: The Hanafite madhhab of the Persian east, the legal formation underlying his later scandals
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'

stops.name: Bestam, the street that takes his name
stops.date_confidence: undated. The move and the renaming are both recorded without years, and the renaming is necessarily later than the move
stops.campa: The family leaves the Mo'bedan quarter and settles among the Arabs, in a street called Wafedan. In time the street stops being called Wafedan. The neighbours rename it Buyadan, after the man who lives there, and the change outlasts every other record of his household. A Zoroastrian's grandson has taken a quarter of an Arab town and given it a Persian name of his own. Sahlaji notes it on the same page as the birth, without comment, as though it were the ordinary thing.
suggested_refs: The Buyadan quarter of Bestam, formerly Wafedan, renamed in his lifetime or shortly after
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji p. 47

stops.name: Bestam, the exchange with Abu Ali al-Sindi
stops.date_confidence: undated. The sources place it in his formation and fix it to no year
stops.campa: A shaykh called Abu Ali al-Sindi comes to Bestam. He cannot read. He does not know the obligatory duties well enough to perform them. And he holds, in pure form, the doctrine of the divine oneness and the mystical realities. So the two men trade. Bayazid teaches him what a child of the Hanafites has by heart, the ablution and the hours of prayer, and takes in exchange the tawhid that will burn the jurist out of him. Sarraj records the whole exchange in two lines, and every argument about where Bayazid's teaching came from begins there.
stops.quote: I sloughed off my self as a snake sloughs off its skin: then I looked into my self and lo! I was He.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bayazid by Sahlaji and by al-Biruni; translation from R. C. Zaehner, Hindu and Muslim Mysticism, p. 98
suggested_refs: Sarraj, Ketab al-loma', pp. 177 and 325, on the exchange of the obligatory duties for the mystical realities
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sarraj, Ketab al-loma', pp. 177, 325
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (al-Sindi described as illiterate)
R. C. Zaehner, Hindu and Muslim Mysticism, p. 98

stops.name: Mansura in Sind, the country the teacher came from
stops.date_confidence: no source places Bayazid here. The pin marks the old Sindhi capital as a representative point for the region his teacher's name points to, nothing more
stops.campa: Al-Sindi means the man from Sind, and Sind is the Indus country, the far eastern rim of the caliphate, where Islam and the older Indian schools share a river. From 1821 the scholars fight over what came up that road. Tholuck proposes a Hindu channel; Nicholson and Horten agree; Ritter half agrees; Zaehner builds the full case twice over. Massignon doubts it and Arberry answers that the imagery is Qur'anic and Sufi and nothing else. Bayazid himself never goes. The quarrel is two centuries old and still open, and it turns on one man who could not write.
suggested_refs: The Tholuck-Zaehner thesis of Indian influence on Bayazid, and the Massignon-Arberry rebuttal
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bowering), summarizing Tholuck 1821, Nicholson 1916, Massignon 1922, Horten 1927, Ritter 1954, Arberry 1957, Zaehner 1957 and 1960

stops.name: Kufa, the pilgrim road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The hajj is attested, this waystation is not; it is the road every Persian pilgrim took, and nothing is recorded of him on it
stops.campa: The Khorasan road runs west out of Qumes toward Rayy, then bends south to the Iraqi cities, and every pilgrim from the Persian east who means to reach the Hijaz comes through Kufa and takes the Darb Zubayda from there. Tradition puts Bayazid on it. Nothing is recorded of what he did in the city of Ali's mosque, and nothing is claimed. Three and a half centuries on, Attar of Nishapur will make the same two turns in the same order, Bastam first and then Kufa, collecting the sayings of the man who went ahead of him down this road.
suggested_refs: The Darb Zubayda, the walled pilgrim road from Kufa to Mecca with its cisterns and halts
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (hajj narrative)
attar.journey.json, stops 'Bastam, at the tomb of Bayazid' and 'Kufa, the mosque of Ali'

stops.name: Fayd, the beggar on the desert road
stops.date_confidence: hagiography, undated. Attar tells it three centuries after the road; the station of Fayd is placed here in Ha'il province, not at the unrelated village of the same name near Mecca
stops.campa: At a station on the desert road, one of the walled halts Zubayda built with cisterns for the pilgrims, an old sick beggar stops him. You are going to circle a house of stone, the man says, when the One who lives in it can be turned toward from where you stand. The story is Attar's, told three hundred years after the road was walked, and no earlier witness puts the beggar on it. The beggar is asking him to attend to the One inside the stone instead of the stone. He listens. Then he goes on to Mecca anyway, and circles the House.
suggested_refs: The Darb Zubayda station of Fayd in Ha'il province, with its cisterns and fort
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya

stops.name: Mecca, the House and the Lord of the House
stops.date_confidence: the pilgrimage is attested by Iranica; the year is unrecorded, and the sources disagree over whether he went once or several times
stops.campa: He circles the Kaaba. Afterward, in the account most often repeated of him, he says that he went round the House and did not see the Lord of the House, only the House. Later, in the cell at Bestam, the direction will reverse: he will claim that the Kaaba circles around him, and turn the qibla from God toward himself. Seven years after his death Hallaj will keep a year's vigil in this same courtyard, and will be crucified at Baghdad for a sentence of the same family as Bayazid's, which nobody ever crucified him for.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram, the fixed point his utterances later invert
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica (pilgrimage attested)
Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya; Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub (the Lord of the House saying, with variant framing)
hallaj.journey.json, stop 'Mecca, a year in the courtyard'

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source isolates this visit; it sits inside the general hajj account and is implied by ninth-century pilgrim practice
stops.campa: North from Mecca to the green-domed mosque, as every pilgrim of the ninth century goes who can afford the extra road. No source separates the visit out; it lies inside the general hajj account and nowhere else. The Prophet's grave lies inside the mosque, under the room where he died. A hadith scholar of Bestam will one day accuse Bayazid of claiming for himself the Night Journey of the man buried here, and will drive him out of his own town over it, and the sentence will stand until the accuser is dead.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina, whose mi'raj the Bestam jurists later accuse him of imitating
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (standard hajj itinerary)
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, following Sahlaji, on the mi'raj accusation

stops.name: Bestam, the mother's threshold
stops.date_confidence: hagiography, undated. Attar tells it and Rumi retells it; there is no earlier witness
stops.campa: He packs to leave again, for the road and the many masters the tradition credits him with, and his mother, old now, asks for water in the night. He does not go. Attar tells the story and Rumi retells it at Konya four hundred years later, giving Bayazid the line that his mother's threshold is his Kaaba. Attar reports over a hundred teachers. The tidy figures, a hundred and thirteen or a hundred and three, trace back to no list at all, and the second of them belongs to a rival claim about how many years he lived.
suggested_refs: Rumi's retelling of the mother's threshold in the Masnavi, the Konya echo of a Bestam anecdote
sources: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya
Rumi, Masnavi-i Ma'navi (later literary echo, not independent attestation)
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (Attar reports 'over one hundred' masters)

stops.name: Bestam, the sealed room
stops.date_confidence: attested practice, undated. Iranica draws it from Attar's chapter without dates
stops.campa: He stops every opening in the room so that no noise can reach him. Sometimes he stands for hours on the points of his toes. Sometimes he sits with his head down on his knees, entirely silent, lifting it only to sigh once. A visitor comes in, looks at him, and goes away again without realising the man is at prayer. Outside this room he keeps a cell, a sawma'a, apart from the houses. He lives between the three, and tells the men who come to argue that his own recollection of God was never the first thing in the room.
stops.quote: I imagined that I recollected God, knew Him, loved Him, and searched for Him. At the end I realized that His recollection preceded mine, His knowledge was prior to mine, His love came before my own, and His search was there before I sought Him.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bayazid in Solami pp. 64-65, Sahlaji p. 96, Esfahani X p. 34, and Attar I p. 170; translation as given in Encyclopaedia Iranica
suggested_refs: The sawma'a, the isolated cell at Bestam where most of his life was spent
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Attar I, pp. 140, 143, 154, 157

stops.name: Bestam, the mouth rinsed before the Name
stops.date_confidence: attested practice, undated
stops.campa: Before he says the name of God in dhekr he rinses his mouth and washes his tongue. He puts a man out of the mosque for standing to pray without a proper ablution. The exactness is the jurist's, kept up long after the jurist has been burned out of him, and it turns inward as easily as out. He tells his own students that after years of hammering at his soul he looked down and found the unbeliever's belt still tied around his waist, woven out of nothing but his satisfaction with his own obedience.
stops.quote: For twelve years I was the blacksmith of my soul... After that I gazed upon my own reflection for a year, and I saw about my waist an infidel girdle of delusion and coquetry and self-regard, because I relied upon my own acts of obedience and approved of my own conduct. For five years further I laboured till that girdle was snapped and I was a Muslim anew.
stops.quote_source: Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, trans. A. J. Arberry, Muslim Saints and Mystics, p. 139
suggested_refs: The zunnar, the girdle worn by non-Muslims under Islamic rule, turned by Bayazid into a figure for self-regard
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Solami, Tabaqat, pp. 62-63; Sahlaji p. 106; Esfahani X p. 35
Attar, trans. Arberry, Muslim Saints and Mystics, p. 139

stops.name: Bestam, glory be to Me
stops.date_confidence: undated. No saying of his carries a year; the sequence in this segment is arrangement, not chronology
stops.campa: The sentence repeated against him for a thousand years is four words of Arabic. Sobhani, ma a'zama sha'ni. It takes the formula the Qur'an reserves for God and applies it to the speaker, and Sarraj, transmitting it, writes down only the first word, as though the rest could not be set on a page. Arberry renders the second half as how great is my dignity, Zaehner as how great is my glory, Schimmel as how great is my majesty. He is credited as the first Sufi to speak this way steadily, year after year, in the sessions and not only under seizure.
stops.quote: Glory be to Me! How great is My Majesty!
stops.quote_source: Sobhani, ma a'zama sha'ni, attributed to Bayazid by Sahlaji; translation from Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam, p. 146
suggested_refs: The shath, the ecstatic utterance, as a genre Bayazid is credited with founding
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'
Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam, p. 146
Zaehner, Hindu and Muslim Mysticism, p. 98 (noting Sarraj records only sobhani)

stops.name: Bestam, there is no God but I
stops.date_confidence: undated
stops.campa: The shahada is the sentence that makes a man a Muslim, and he takes it apart and sets his own pronoun where the name of God stands. To the men listening in the mosque of Bestam it is either the highest thing anyone has said in that language or it is apostasy, and there is no third reading available. He says also that all human beings are his servants except the one he is speaking to, and that all creatures are his. Sahlaji writes them down two centuries later and does not soften a word.
stops.quote: I am I; there is no God but I; so worship me!
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bayazid in Sahlaji, pp. 119 and 122, cited in Gerhard Bowering, 'Bestami, Bayazid,' Encyclopaedia Iranica
suggested_refs: Sahlaji's Ketab al-nur as the unsoftened record of the ecstatic sayings
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji pp. 119, 122

stops.name: Bestam, the muezzin answered
stops.date_confidence: undated
stops.campa: From the minaret the call goes up, God is great. From the street below Bayazid answers, I am greater. He takes the Qur'anic verse on the firmness of God's grasp and rewrites it in the first person, making his own hold the firmer of the two. He claims to contain in himself the seven abdal, the hidden substitute-saints on whom the age is said to rest, and to be the preserved tablet, and the shoreless ocean, and the throne. Ebn al-Jawzi will collect these same lines later, as a catalogue of the devil's deceptions.
stops.quote: By my life, my grasp is firmer than His.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bayazid in Ruzbehan Baqli, Sharh-e shathiyat, p. 101, and Sahlaji p. 111, cited in Encyclopaedia Iranica
suggested_refs: Ebn al-Jawzi's Talbis Eblis, which preserves the sayings by condemning them
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Ruzbehan Baqli p. 101; Sahlaji pp. 80, 111, 113; Esfahani X p. 37; Ebn al-Jawzi p. 333; Attar I p. 171

stops.name: Bestam, the wish for hell
stops.date_confidence: undated
stops.campa: He asks to be sent to hell, on the ground that being singled out for damnation would still be a mark of God's attention, and asks further to be made so vast on arrival that no other soul can be fitted in beside him. Then he says that hell would go out if he looked at it, and that the hem of his coat would smother it. The men who preserve these lines are mostly hostile witnesses. Ebn al-Jawzi files them under delusion, and it is because his enemies quoted him that the words survive at all.
suggested_refs: The transmission of the shathiyat through hostile compilers, chiefly Ebn al-Jawzi
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Ebn al-Jawzi pp. 329, 331, 334; Sahlaji pp. 114-15

stops.name: Bestam, before the jurists
stops.date_confidence: the hostility of the ulama and the resulting exile are attested by Iranica; no year, no count, and no duration is recorded
stops.campa: The sayings are carried to the ulama of the town as accusations of unbelief. No court record survives and he is not killed; half a century later Hallaj will be, at Baghdad, for a sentence of the same kind. What Bestam does instead is put him out. Iranica states the exile plainly and gives it neither a length nor a number. The seven expulsions of popular tradition appear in none of the sources that matter; that figure, like his birth year, is somebody's later arithmetic.
suggested_refs: The Bestam ulama's accusations of unbelief, the local pressure behind the exiles
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'
Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya; Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub
hallaj.journey.json (the same charge, carried to execution)

stops.name: Gorgan, the years in Jurjan
stops.date_confidence: the exile is attested and the year is not. Sahlaji, via the TDV article, gives the sequence: the accusation, then the hajj, then Jurjan, then a return only after the accuser's death
stops.campa: A hadith scholar accuses him of claiming for himself an ascension like the Prophet's, and Bestam becomes unlivable. He performs the pilgrimage, then goes west along the Caspian slope into Jurjan, the wet country under the forest where the Alborz comes down toward the sea, and stays. Of all the times the town drives him out, this is the only one whose destination anybody thought to write down. He waits there. The condition of his return is not a pardon and not a recantation. It is a funeral.
suggested_refs: Jurjan, the Caspian province that sheltered him during the longest recorded exile
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, following Sahlaji
Encyclopaedia Iranica (repeated short exiles attested without destinations)

stops.name: Bestam, the accuser dies
stops.date_confidence: undated. The return is attested only as consequent on the accuser's death
stops.campa: The scholar who denounced him dies, and Bayazid comes home. Nothing has been settled by the death and nothing is retracted. He goes back to the house, the mosque, and the cell, resumes the teaching sessions, and receives the men who come from Balkh and Nishapur and Egypt to argue. The sayings continue and so does the hostility, and he will be put out again. The town that expelled him will end by naming a street after him and building its one monument over his grave.
suggested_refs: The pattern of expulsion and return that structures his years at Bestam
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, following Sahlaji
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'

stops.name: Bestam, the ascent through the seven heavens
stops.date_confidence: the vision is undated and reported by him in the first person; the text of it is attested by Sarraj (d. 378/988) and elaborated in a version dated 395/1005
stops.campa: He tells it in the first person. He goes up through the seven heavens as the Prophet went, is met at each level by angels offering him kingdoms and birds of light, refuses every offer, comes near the throne, and comes back. Sarraj has the account written down by the end of the tenth century. In 1005 a longer and more decorated version begins circulating under Junayd's name, compiled by a certain Abu'l-Qasem, and the attribution is wrong. Ibn Arabi will still be measuring himself against it at Damascus four hundred years on.
suggested_refs: The Resalat al-qasd ela'llah, the embellished mi'raj of 395/1005, wrongly ascribed to Junayd
sources: Sarraj, Kitab al-Luma'
Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing R. A. Nicholson, 'An Early Arabic Version of the Mi'raj of Abu Yazid al-Bistami,' Islamica 2 (1926), pp. 402-15

stops.name: Bestam, the emissary from Egypt
stops.date_confidence: attested visits, undated. Dhu'l-Nun dies 245/860, Ahmad b. Khezruya 240/854, which brackets them loosely
stops.campa: Dhu'l-Nun the Egyptian, who is doing at Cairo something close to what Bayazid is doing in Qumes, sends a man across the whole width of the caliphate to put a question to him and carry back the answer. Ahmad ibn Khezruya of Balkh turns aside on his own pilgrimage to sit with him. The recluse who stops up his windows against noise keeps a correspondence running from Cairo to Balkh, and the men who make that journey carry his sentences home with them, which is how the sayings first leave Qumes.
suggested_refs: The ninth-century correspondence network linking Bestam, Balkh, Nishapur, Baghdad, and Cairo
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Qushayri p. 38; Hojviri pp. 322, 331-32; Sahlaji pp. 65, 73, 117, 131; Attar I p. 156

stops.name: Nishapur, the letters on the oceans of love
stops.date_confidence: attested exchange, undated. Yahya is a native of Rayy but preached and died at Nishapur in 871, so the pin follows him rather than his birthplace
stops.campa: Yahya ibn Mu'adh, born at Rayy and preaching now at Nishapur, writes to Bestam: what do you say of one who drinks a single drop of the ocean of love and becomes intoxicated? The answer that comes back makes the question look temperate. Hujwiri, telling it, notes the reversal nobody expects, that the famous preacher of hope is speaking here for sobriety and the recluse of Bestam for drunkenness. Yahya dies at Nishapur in his forties, four years before the date most scholars give for Bayazid's own death.
stops.quote: What do you say of one who, if all the oceans in the world were filled with the wine of love, would drink them all and still cry for more to slake his thirst?
stops.quote_source: Bayazid's written reply to Yahya ibn Mu'adh, in Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. R. A. Nicholson, p. 187
suggested_refs: Hujwiri's chapter on the Tayfuris, where the exchange with Yahya ibn Mu'adh is preserved
sources: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. Nicholson, p. 187
Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji p. 136; Esfahani, Helyat al-awliya X p. 40; Attar I pp. 143-44
Abu Nu'aym, Hilyat al-Awliya 10:40, via Schimmel p. 51 (a second recension of the same exchange)

stops.name: Dvin, the mission sent into Armenia
stops.date_confidence: the sending is attested by Sam'ani and Sahlaji; no town is named in any source, and this pin marks the medieval Armenian capital as a representative point only
stops.campa: He sends Abu Musa al-Dabili, a disciple of Abd al-Rahim ibn Yahya al-Dabili, back into his own country to plant Sufism there. Armenia is Christian ground under Muslim governors, weeks north-west of Bestam across the plateau. Sam'ani records the sending. Nobody records the town, or whether the man arrived, or what he found when he did. It is the furthest the teaching of a man who barely leaves one street travels in his own lifetime, and it travels the whole way in somebody else's feet.
suggested_refs: Sam'ani's Ansab, V p. 313, on the Dabili mission into Armenia
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sam'ani (ed. Yamani) V p. 313; Sahlaji pp. 54-55

stops.name: Bestam, four years old
stops.date_confidence: undated saying, placed here for the sequence. Commonly misattributed to Attar; the traceable source is Hujwiri
stops.campa: Somebody asks the old man his age and he answers, four. Pressed on it, he gives the arithmetic: for seventy years the world stood between him and God, and those years are not counted, because a man is not alive during them. He has been alive four. It concedes what none of the other sayings concede, that the seventy years happened and that they were his. Hujwiri sets it in the chapter on contemplation rather than among the scandals, and it is Hujwiri, not Attar, who has it.
stops.quote: I have been veiled (from God) by this world for seventy years, but I have seen Him during the last four years: the period in which one is veiled does not belong to one's life.
stops.quote_source: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. R. A. Nicholson, p. 331, in the chapter on contemplation
suggested_refs: Nicholson's Kashf al-Mahjub p. 331, the traceable source for a saying usually credited to Attar
sources: Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, trans. Nicholson, p. 331
R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), chapter on contemplation

stops.name: Bestam, the death
stops.date_confidence: two dates stand in the sources and neither is chosen. 234/848, recorded by Sahlaji p. 63 and by Solami p. 60 on the authority of Ja'far Kholdi, has the better circumstantial fit; 261/875, on a family esnad, is commonly accepted by scholars and is the one pinned here
stops.campa: He dies in Bestam, in the town he was born in and expelled from and returned to, past seventy years of age. On the year the sources split cleanly and stay split. Sahlaji, who knows more about him than anybody, gives 848. The family chain his own nephew began gives 875, and the scholars follow the family. The meetings with Shaqiq of Balkh and Ahmad ibn Khezruya pull hard toward the earlier year. Bowering sets the two side by side, notes the strain, and declines to choose between them.
suggested_refs: The two death dates, 234/848 and 261/875, and the transmission chains behind each
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bowering), summarizing Sahlaji p. 63 and Solami, Tabaqat, p. 60
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (Sahlaji: born 161/777, died aged 73 in 234/848)

stops.name: Bestam, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested. The burial place is the one fact about him no source disputes
stops.campa: They bury him at Bestam. Within a generation or two people are coming to the grave, and by the tenth century a small body of his followers keeps itself together around it and takes his name. He leaves no book. Some five hundred of his sayings are held in other men's memories, and the street outside carries his name. The ground he is under will draw the Il-khanids and Attar of Nishapur and every later Naqshbandi lineage-maker into this one corner of Qumes.
suggested_refs: The grave at Bestam, nucleus of the Tayfuriya and later of the whole shrine complex
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'
Wikipedia, 'Bastam'

stops.name: Bestam, the nephew begins the chain
stops.date_confidence: the two transmission lines are attested; their starting years are not recorded
stops.campa: Abu Musa Isa ibn Adam, his nephew, who waited on him and heard him daily, begins reciting the sayings to whoever will take them down, and the family line of transmission starts. A second line runs through the visitors: Ebrahim Heravi, called Satanba, and Ahmad ibn Khezruya of Balkh. Roughly five hundred sayings survive between them. Every word attributed to Bayazid reaches the world through one of these two chains, and both of them begin only after he has stopped speaking.
suggested_refs: The family esnad through Abu Musa Isa b. Adam, and the visitors' line through Heravi and Ibn Khezruya
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji pp. 108-109, 122-23; Esfahani X pp. 43-44; Sahlaji p. 56

stops.name: Baghdad, Junayd turns the Persian into Arabic
stops.date_confidence: the translation is attested on the family esnad; the year is not. Junayd dies in 298/910
stops.campa: Junayd of Baghdad takes the sayings, spoken in Persian, and puts them into Arabic, and by doing so becomes the man through whom the Arabic-reading world will hear Bayazid forever after. The two never met. Iranica states it flatly: no record exists of any meeting, though Bayazid was on familiar terms with Sari al-Saqati, who was Junayd's uncle and his teacher. The school that canonises him has no contact with him. Hujwiri will name the two parties after them, the drunken Tayfuriya against the sober Junaydiya, and set them at odds for good.
suggested_refs: Hojviri, Kashf al-mahjub, pp. 228-35, on the Tayfuriya of intoxication against the Junaydiya of sobriety
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Sahlaji pp. 81, 108-109, 122-23
Hojviri, Kashf al-mahjub, pp. 228-35

stops.name: Kharaqan, the disciple who came a century late
stops.date_confidence: attested. Kharaqani is born 352/963 and dies 425/1033, eighty-eight years after Bayazid's burial, which is precisely why the transmission has to be uwaysi
stops.campa: Abu'l-Hasan of Kharaqan is born eighty-eight years after Bayazid is buried, in a village a day's walk from Bestam, and takes him for his master anyway. He walks to the tomb again and again and receives his instruction there, out of the ground, in the manner the Sufis call uwaysi: taught by a man you cannot meet. Iran accepts him as the heir. Through his own pupil Abu Ali al-Farmadi the line runs on into the chain the Naqshbandi order will one day claim, so that an order founded centuries later begins its silsila at a grave in Qumes.
suggested_refs: The village of Qaleh Now-e Kharaqan in Semnan province, and the uwaysi transmission from a grave
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Attar II pp. 201-55; Minovi pp. 11, 15, 17-26, 29-30, 34-36
Wikipedia, 'Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani' (b. 352/963, d. 425/1033)

stops.name: Bestam, Sahlaji compiles the Book of Light
stops.date_confidence: Sahlaji lives 389-476 AH, 998-1084 CE; the compilation is placed in the middle of his working life and is not separately dated
stops.campa: Abu'l-Fadl Muhammad ibn Ali Sahlaji, whose life spans eighty-six years of the eleventh century, gathers what the two chains carried and writes the Ketab al-nur men kalemat Abi Tayfur, the Book of Light from the Words of Abu Tayfur. He draws on Dastani, and on Ibn Babuya of Shiraz, who wrote the life of Hallaj. It is the most detailed source there is. The household, the quarter, the teachers, the exiles, and both rival death dates all reach modern scholarship through this one book.
suggested_refs: Sahlaji, Ketab al-nur men kalemat Abi Tayfur, the single indispensable source for Bayazid
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid' (Sahlaji 389-476/998-1084, drawing on Dastani d. 417/1026 and Ibn Babuya Shirazi d. 442/1050)

stops.name: Shiraz, Ruzbihan defends the ecstatic sayings
stops.date_confidence: attested. Ruzbihan lives 1128-1209, returns to Shiraz in 1165, and completes the Sharh-i Shathiyat in 1174
stops.campa: Ruzbihan Baqli, nine years back in Shiraz, finishes the Sharh-i Shathiyat, a defence of the ecstatic sayings of the early Sufis. Hallaj is his chief example and Bayazid stands beside him. The argument is that these sentences are not claims a man makes about himself but sounds made through a man once the self has got out of the way, so that reading them as ordinary speech is a mistake about what kind of speech they are. Three hundred years after Bestam, the sayings finally have a lawyer.
suggested_refs: Ruzbihan Baqli, Sharh-i Shathiyat, completed at Shiraz in 1174
sources: Standard scholarship on Ruzbihan Baqli's Sharh-i Shathiyat
Wikipedia, 'Ruzbihan Baqli' (Hallaj as the primary example of the genre)

stops.name: Bastam, Attar kneels at the tomb
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The date follows the corpus reconstruction of Attar's journey in attar.journey.json
stops.campa: West of Nishapur, turning off the road toward Iraq and Arabia, Attar comes to Bastam and kneels a long time at the grave, gathering sayings for a book of the lives of the saints that he has not yet conceived. Bayazid will get one of the two longest chapters in it. Back at the shop in Shadiyakh the notebooks fill with him, beside Hallaj and Rabia and a hundred lesser names, and when Attar writes the conference of the birds it is this voice, self-annihilated, that the thirty birds hear coming out of the Simurgh.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Bayazid at Bastam, given one of the two longest lives in Attar's Tazkirat al-Awliya
sources: attar.journey.json, stops 'Bastam, at the tomb of Bayazid' (1176) and 'Shadiyakh, return to the shop, the notebooks of the road' (1186)

stops.name: Damascus, Ibn Arabi finishes the Meccan Revelations
stops.date_confidence: the book's dates are attested: begun at Mecca 1202, first draft December 1231, second recension 1238 at Damascus. That the Futuhat discusses Bayazid's ascension is standard in the scholarship but was not confirmable in reachable sources
stops.campa: Ibn Arabi begins the Futuhat al-Makkiyya at Mecca in 1202 and completes the second recension at Damascus in 1238, two years before he is buried on the slope of Qasiyun. Bayazid's ascension sits inside it as a case to be measured against his own account of the ascent: the Persian recluse's seven heavens, read by an Andalusian who has climbed them by another route. Six centuries later Emir Abdelkader will be laid in the ground beside him, having spent his last decades writing commentary on this book.
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's tomb at Salihiyya on Qasiyun, where the Futuhat was completed and where Abdelkader was later buried
sources: Claude Addas, via Wikipedia, 'Ibn Arabi' (composition dates of the Futuhat)

stops.name: Konya, Shams seizes the bridle
stops.date_confidence: traditional, per Aflaki and Sultan Walad; the corpus fixes the date at 29 November 1244 in rumi.journey.json
stops.campa: Outside the Inn of the Sugar Merchants a dervish in black felt catches the bridle of the most respected teacher in Konya and asks him a question with two names in it. Which is greater: Muhammad, who said we have not known You as You should be known, or Bayazid, who said glory be to me, how great is my station? Rumi answers that the Prophet's unknowing surpasses all Bayazid's claiming, and faints in the road at the force of his own answer. Everything Rumi becomes afterward turns on a sentence spoken at Bestam four hundred years before.
stops.quote: The Prophet's 'we have not known You as You should be known' surpasses Bayazid's 'glory be to me' — for Bayazid's thirst was small enough to be satisfied by a single drop, and he cried that he was full, while the Prophet's vessel could never be filled, and he thirsted on.
stops.quote_source: The traditional form of Rumi's answer to Shams of Tabriz, transmitted in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, and Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama
suggested_refs: The Sekerciler Han site in Konya's old bazaar, traditional site of the meeting between Rumi and Shams

stops.name: Bestam, Oljeitu raises the dome
stops.date_confidence: attested, 713 AH / 1313 CE, per Encyclopaedia Iranica; the single most specific construction date in the whole complex
stops.campa: The Il-khanid ruler Muhammad Khodabanda, called Oljeitu, a Mongol convert who has changed religion more than once already, builds a dome over the grave. The complex around it goes on accreting for six hundred years: the Jami mosque, a khanqah, the shrine of Mohammad ibn Ja'far al-Sadiq, and the Kashaneh, a twenty-four metre tower with thirty sides, inscribed with the year 700, which Godard assigns to Ghazan although the inscription names Oljeitu too. The man who owned nothing gets a monument by instalments.
suggested_refs: The Kashaneh tower at Bastam, thirty-sided, inscribed 700 AH, attributed variously to Ghazan and Oljeitu
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bestami, Bayazid'
Wikipedia, 'Bastam' (Kashaneh tower, Seljuk to Qajar phases)

stops.name: Kirikhan, the second tomb
stops.date_confidence: undated local tradition of the Ottoman period. The year is a placeholder; the foundation date of the complex is not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: In the Amanus foothills of Hatay, some sixteen hundred and seventy kilometres west of Bestam, a shrine complex stands inside the ruins of the crusader castle of Darb-i Sak, at Alabeyli village on the road from Kirikhan to Hassa. It carries his name and is venerated as his tomb. Nearby lies a Sheikh Isa, said locally to be his descendant, which is very likely how the name walked this far. No source reconciles the two graves, and neither tradition has ever felt the want of one.
suggested_refs: The Beyazid-i Bestami Kulliyesi at Alabeyli, built within the walls of Darb-i Sak castle
sources: Turkish Wikipedia, 'Beyazid-i Bestami Kulliyesi'
Wikipedia, 'Kirikhan'

stops.name: Chittagong, the shrine at Nasirabad
stops.date_confidence: the sarcophagus is uncovered in 1831 and the mosque is Mughal, under Aurangzeb; local tradition dates the site to c. 850, and no evidence places Bayazid anywhere in Bengal
stops.campa: On a hillock outside Chittagong a sarcophagus is uncovered in 1831, at a site local tradition has long called his, with a three-domed mosque raised over it under Aurangzeb. In the tank below live black softshell turtles, held to be evil spirits that incurred the saint's anger, and the species survives nowhere else on earth: the register lists it as extinct in the wild. Nothing places Bayazid within two thousand miles of Bengal. Scholars call the tomb a jawab, an answering tomb, built to reply to a grave somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The tank of Nilssonia nigricans at the Nasirabad shrine, a species listed extinct in the wild since 2002
sources: Wikipedia, 'Shrine of Bayazid Bostami' (coordinates, 1831 sarcophagus, jawab hypothesis, no evidence of a visit)
Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing M. Abdur Rabb, The Life, Thought and Historical Importance of Abu Yazid al-Bistami (Dacca, 1971), p. 79

stops.name: Paris, Massignon in the lexicon
stops.date_confidence: attested publication year
stops.campa: Louis Massignon, who has spent his working life inside the trial of Hallaj, publishes the Essai sur les origines du lexique technique de la mystique musulmane and treats Bayazid's vocabulary of ecstasy as evidence for how the Arabic language of mysticism was built. The same year, he refuses Tholuck's Indian hypothesis. Nicholson has already argued the other side and will print the early Arabic text of Bayazid's ascension four years later. The quarrel over one unlettered teacher from Sind outlives every man who enters it.
suggested_refs: Massignon, Essai sur les origines du lexique technique de la mystique musulmane (Paris, 1922)
sources: Louis Massignon, Essai sur les origines du lexique technique de la mystique musulmane (Paris, 1922)
Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bowering) on the Indian-influence debate

stops.name: Albany, Words of Ecstasy
stops.date_confidence: attested publication year
stops.campa: Carl Ernst publishes Words of Ecstasy in Sufism, the first full English study of the shath as a genre with rules of its own, and Bayazid stands at its head as the man who made ecstatic utterance a method instead of an accident. Four years later Abdelwahab Meddeb brings the sayings into French as Les dits de Bistami. The five hundred fragments a nephew once recited from memory at Bestam are now a subject with a bibliography, in languages nobody in Qumes had heard of.
suggested_refs: Carl W. Ernst, Words of Ecstasy in Sufism (SUNY Press, 1985); Abdelwahab Meddeb, Les dits de Bistami (Paris, 1989)
sources: Carl W. Ernst, Words of Ecstasy in Sufism (State University of New York Press, Albany, 1985)
Abdelwahab Meddeb, Les dits de Bistami (Paris, 1989)

stops.name: Bestam, the shrine today
stops.date_confidence: present state of the site in Semnan province, Iran
stops.campa: The complex still stands in Semnan province and still takes pilgrims: tomb, mosque, khanqah, the thirty-sided tower, a millennium of masonry laid over one grave. The street is still called Buyadan. He wrote nothing down in his own hand, and the sources still offer two years for his death, 848 and 875, with no way given of choosing between them. The town holds the ground he is in, and four words of Arabic that the Persian language has not managed to put down since.
stops.quote: The thing we tell of can never be found by seeking, yet only seekers find it.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bayazid in R. A. Nicholson, Translations of Eastern Poetry and Prose (Cambridge, 1922), p. 140
suggested_refs: The Bayazid Bastami shrine complex at Bastam, Semnan province, active pilgrimage site
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bastam'
